chunks.text: A Database is a shared collection of logically related data (and a description of this data), designed to meet the information needs of an organization. It is a single, large repository of data used simultaneously by many departments. A Database Management System (DBMS) is a software system that enables users to define, create, and maintain the database and that provides controlled access to this database.

The Database Approach involves two key languages: (1) Data Definition Language (DDL) — permits specification of data types, structures, and any data constraints; all specifications are stored in the database. (2) Data Manipulation Language (DML) — provides a general inquiry facility (query language) for the data.

Controlled access to a database in the DBMS approach may include: a security system, an integrity system, a concurrency control system, a recovery control system, a user-accessible catalogue, and a view mechanism that provides users with only the data they want or need to use.

A view allows each user to have his or her own view of the database; it is essentially some subset of the database. Benefits of views include: reducing complexity, providing a level of security, providing a mechanism to customize the appearance of the database, and presenting a consistent, unchanging picture of the database structure even if the underlying database is changed.

The components of the DBMS environment are: (1) Hardware — can range from a PC to a network of computers. (2) Software — includes the DBMS, operating system, network software if necessary, and application programs. (3) Data — used by the organization and a description of this data; the structure of the database is called the schema. (4) Procedures — instructions and rules for the design and use of the database, such as how to log on, make backups, handle failures, and change table structures. (5) People — the various roles involved in using and managing the database.

Roles in the Database Environment include: Database Administrator (DBA) — manages the DBMS's use and ensures its proper function; Database Designers (Logical and Physical) — design the database structure, how and in what format data will be stored, and the relationships between data items; System Administrator — oversees the database system's general operations; Systems Analysts and Programmers — design and implement application programs, data entry screens, and reports; End Users (naive and sophisticated, e.g., clerks, supervisors, managers) — use the application programs to run the organization's daily operations.
Databases can be located in two ways: (1) Centralized — supports data located at a single site. (2) Distributed — supports data distributed across several sites.

Advantages of DBMSs include: control of data redundancy, improved data integrity, improved security, improved data accessibility, improved maintenance, increased concurrency, and improved backup and recovery services. Disadvantages include: complexity, size, cost of the DBMS, and cost of conversion.
